parole.testo: From an onomatopoeic base *liz-. Or, possibly influenced by or of Germanic origin, from Frankish *slīdan; compare English slide. Cognate with Portuguese deslizar.
From a Germanic language, probably Frankish *falda (“to fold”), related to Old High German faldan (“to fold”), English fold, all from Proto-West Germanic *falþan. Doublet of halda.
Unknown, perhaps a Germanic (possibly Frankish) borrowing, from Proto-West Germanic *felt. See also Italian and Portuguese felpa, Occitan feupo, Catalan pelfa.

Of Germanic origin; compare Spanish guadañar (“to mow”). Probably from Frankish *waiþanjan (“to pasture, forage”), from Proto-Germanic *waiþō (“hunt, pasture, food”), or derived from guadañar. Cognate with Old High German weidanōn (“to hunt, forage for food”, whence German weiden), Middle English wa

parole.significato: to give shelter, protect, preserve from harm
parole.testo: From guarir, a Germanic borrowing from Frankish *warjan (“to protect”).

Of Germanic origin, from Frankish *warjan, related to guarecer and garita. In 2014, the Nicolás Maduro government began using the word with its current definition, referring to opposition protests that they thought were childish. For Maduro supporters, the word has strongly negative connotations. Ho
From Germanic, from Frankish *krampa or Gothic *𐌺𐍂𐌰𐌼𐍀𐌰 (*krampa), both from Proto-Germanic *krampō. See also Old High German kramph, English cramp, French crampe. Doublet of calambre.

parole.significato: snout (long, projecting nose, mouth and jaw of a beast)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Germanic language, from Frankish *trumpa or Old High German trumpa, trumba, of imitative origin, similar to English drum.
